title: Bell and Room
premise: Gideon Sandoval returns to the family farmhouse to bury his twin sister Odile, who died three years ago—yet he has spent those same three years telling himself the sounds in his walls were pipes, raccoons, settling wood. On the porch waits Bell, the imaginary friend they invented as children, unchanged by time and impatient about a promise made in the frost of one terrible winter. As night falls, Gideon learns that one twin was 'invited in' long ago, that survival back then came at a price paid on credit, and that the debt has come due to whichever sibling is still breathing. To last until sunrise, Gideon must finally remember what really happened the winter Odile stopped speaking—and choose whether to pay the inheritance himself or let it pass, unfinished, to whatever comes after him.
about_author: Orsen Coldharbour is the pen name of a former rural coroner's assistant who spent a decade cataloguing deaths in farming counties where records went back further than anyone liked. They write horror about houses that keep accounts, and claim never to write after dark.

chapters.title: The Wrong Grave
chapters.summary: Gideon arrives at the farmhouse with an urn and a lawyer's letter confirming Odile died three years ago; the funeral home insists the paperwork has always been correct. POV: Gideon, close third. The emotional beat is dissonant grief—he mourns someone whose death date contradicts his own memory of her phone calls.

chapters.title: Porch Light
chapters.summary: At dusk, Gideon finds Bell sitting on the porch steps exactly as they left him at age nine—same corduroy coat, same too-wide smile. Bell says he's been waiting for 'the one who stayed.' POV: Gideon. The beat shifts from uncanny dread to a horrible childhood warmth, because part of Gideon is glad.

chapters.title: Inventory of Noises
chapters.summary: Gideon catalogs three years of sounds—the scratching behind the pantry, footsteps upstairs when no one is there—and realizes they began the week Odile 'died.' POV: Gideon, intercut with diary fragments from their mother. The beat is mounting rationalization collapsing into evidence.

chapters.title: What We Invited
chapters.summary: Through a child's drawing and a scorched page of the family Bible, Gideon reconstructs the winter ritual: two children, one bargain, something under the ice that asked to be invited in. POV: Gideon with flashback chapters in child voice. The beat is dawning complicity—they weren't victims; they were volunteers.

chapters.title: Odile's Room
chapters.summary: Gideon enters the sealed bedroom and finds it preserved since childhood—except fresh frost ferns bloom across the window each hour, spelling words. Bell appears inside, gentle, explaining that rooms hold what was promised in them. POV: Gideon. The beat is tenderness curdling into entrapment as the door won't reopen.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Remembers
chapters.summary: Escaping through a window, Gideon seeks elderly neighbor Hattie Voss, who reveals the Sandovals' bargain was inherited—the house has taken a child every generation, and parents chose which twin to give. POV: alternating Gideon/Hattie. The beat is generational horror: his parents did this deliberately.

chapters.title: Three Years of Her
chapters.summary: Gideon confronts the truth of the missing years: the phone calls he remembers were never real; Odile has been in the house, in the walls, kept warm by the thing that wears Bell's face. POV: Gideon, fracturing between memory and revelation. The beat is guilt weaponized—the entity offers him the memories back, one per concession.

chapters.title: Terms of Inheritance
chapters.summary: Bell lays out the terms plainly: the debt passes to blood, and Gideon can pay it, defer it to a future child, or finish what Odile started and take her place willingly. POV: Gideon. The beat is the seduction of surrender—staying invisible forever, safe, warm, beside his sister.

chapters.title: Frostwork
chapters.summary: Climax: as the coldest hour approaches, Gideon runs the house's circuit one last time, un-inviting room by room using the ritual reversed—but the final threshold requires a true name freely given, and the entity offers Odile's voice as bait. POV: Gideon. The beat is desperate agency against a contract designed to be unwinnable.

chapters.title: Sunrise Pattern
chapters.summary: Dawn breaks over a house emptied of everything but frost—and one set of footprints leading away, two sets leading nowhere. Gideon buries the urn empty, keeps the diary, and drives off carrying the deferred debt like a heartbeat. POV: Gideon, then a brief coda in second person addressing the reader. The beat is survival without absolution: the price wasn't cancelled, only postponed.
